sections.h2: When are New Rochelle property taxes due?
sections.html:
New Rochelle homeowners face four separate deadlines a year, because four taxing bodies (the city, Westchester County, the schools and the public library) each bill on their own calendar. The City Tax Department collects all four, and a payment that arrives after that month ends picks up interest and penalties, according to the city's Property Tax Schedule.

Property tax bills collected by the New Rochelle Tax Department
BillDue on or beforePeriod it covers
City taxJanuary 31January 1 to December 31
County taxJune 30January 1 to December 31
School and library, first halfSeptember 30July 1 to December 31
School and library, second halfMarch 31January 1 to June 30

Source: City of New Rochelle, Property Tax Schedule page.

The school and library year runs July to June while the city and county bills follow the calendar year. A closing date that falls mid-year therefore lands in a different slice of each bill. Ask the closing attorney or title company to adjust each of the four bills separately.

sections.h2: Which office sends the New Rochelle tax bill?
sections.html:
The City of New Rochelle Tax Department sends the bills and takes the payments for the city, Westchester County, the New Rochelle City School District and the New Rochelle Public Library. Assessments come from a different office, the Bureau of Assessments inside the Finance Department, which prepares the assessment roll that every one of those bills is built on.

  • Assessor's Office: 515 North Avenue, New Rochelle, NY 10801, weekday hours of 8:30 am until 4:30 pm, telephone (914) 654-2052.
  • Online: the city runs a payment portal that accepts cards and e-checks. Convenience fees apply.
  • In person: the Tax Office is on the ground floor of City Hall at the same North Avenue address.
  • By mail: payable to Tax Collector New Rochelle, with the block and lot number written on the check. The city advises against paying through personal online banking.
  • Direct debit: the city can draw payments automatically from a checking or money market account once you return its authorization form.

Two web tools show parcel data. CitySquared offers mapping, parcel basics and building permit information, and the SDG Property Information portal adds photos and tax history. The city site does not publish a single tax rate for homeowners, so ask the Tax Department about the rate on your own parcel.

sections.h2: What is it like to own and sell a house in New Rochelle?
sections.html:
New Rochelle sits on Long Island Sound at the southeastern point of continental New York, about two miles north of Pelham Bay Park in the Bronx. The city is shaped like a long triangle, roughly ten miles from north to south and 1.5 miles across at its widest, and its land and water together measure 13.2 square miles, according to Wikipedia.

French Huguenot families founded the settlement in 1688, and the village and town merged into one city under a charter signed in 1899. Planned neighborhoods such as Rochelle Park earned it the nickname "City of Homes." The Metro-North station and the New Roc City complex downtown are products of the late twentieth century rebuilding.

Census Bureau QuickFacts gives the current picture for a seller:

  • Population estimated at 85,864 on July 1, 2025, up 7.7 percent from the 2020 base.
  • 31,684 households, with 53.7 percent of housing units owner-occupied.
  • A typical owned home valued at $702,500 over 2020 to 2024, with gross rent at a median of $1,917.
  • Average commute of 32.5 minutes each way.

Water is part of life here. The city has a page for owners with chronic flooding, and an owner whose home is damaged enough to lower its value, with repairs not done by December 1, can contact the assessor in April to arrange an inspection.

sections.h2: How does the New Rochelle assessment calendar work?
sections.html:
The year turns on December 1, the taxable status date. Every property is assessed on its condition that day, and December 1 is also the deadline for filing exemption applications with the Assessor's Office, in person or by mail to 515 North Avenue.

  • December 1: taxable status date and exemption deadline.
  • February 1: the tentative assessment roll is published.
  • Third Tuesday in February: Grievance Day.
  • April 1: the final assessment roll. A changed assessment shows up in the billing cycle that begins September 1.

The city has not run a citywide reassessment since 1956, so values on the roll rarely track the market sale prices you see around town. Renovations are the exception. Work finished in a given year is reviewed as of that year's December 1 and any new figure appears on the next February roll. A homeowner planning a kitchen or an addition before listing can ask the City Appraiser for an estimate of the effect.

sections.h2: How do I file a grievance on my New Rochelle assessment?
sections.html:
File Form RP-524 with the Assessor's Office between February 1 and the third Tuesday in February. The city's grievance page says applications outside that window cannot be accepted.

  • Look at your tentative roll entry on or after February 1, which shows the assessed value and the assessor's estimate of market value.
  • Gather at least three recent arm's length sales of similar homes close by, matched on size, style, age, condition and lot.
  • Submit the original application in person or by mail. Email and fax copies are refused.
  • File one application for each parcel if you own more than one or your property spans several lots.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office for a hearing time with the Board of Assessment Review after the form is in.

The board is made up of residents appointed by the City Council, and no assessor staff sit on it. If your assessment is fair but the bill still feels heavy, the assessor cannot help, since tax rates are set by the council, the school district and the county legislature. After the grievance stage, New York offers Small Claims Assessment Review to most homeowners, and the state says you must go through the local grievance first.

sections.h2: Which exemptions and STAR benefits apply in New Rochelle?
sections.html:
A new owner who applies for STAR receives it as a check or direct deposit from the state. You register with New York State at tax.ny.gov/star, and the credit requires a primary residence and combined income of all owners and spouses of $500,000 or less.

The older Basic STAR exemption stays in place for people who applied before May 1, 2015, with a combined income under $250,000, and its savings have been capped since 2019. Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 or older within the state income limit, and the state now moves eligible owners over without a new application. Other exemptions are filed with the New Rochelle assessor by December 1.

When you sell, the state asks you to close your STAR registration. Your buyer registers as a new owner of the home.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid New Rochelle tax when I sell?
sections.html:
Open balances have to be settled as part of the sale, so start by asking the Tax Department for a statement of every unpaid bill on the parcel. Check the city's fee lists as well, because unpaid false alarm charges move onto the next city tax bill after September 30, and restored to roll, sidewalk repair and property maintenance charges move over after December 1.

The deed itself is recorded with the Westchester County Clerk, not at City Hall. The city assessor says ownership records cannot be changed at the city level and points owners to an attorney who files the papers with the county clerk. If you are behind on taxes, tell your closing attorney or title company early so the payoff figures are ready before the closing date.

faqs.q: Which office handles New Rochelle assessment questions?
faqs.a: The Assessor's Office at 515 North Avenue, which can be reached at (914) 654-2052 on weekdays. It answers questions about assessed value, exemptions and grievance forms but has no say over the tax rate.

faqs.q: When is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?
faqs.a: It falls on the third Tuesday in February. Applications can be filed from February 1 through that Tuesday, and the tentative roll comes out on February 1.

faqs.q: Can I pay a New Rochelle tax bill with a credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, through the city's online payment portal, which also takes e-checks. Convenience fees apply. You can also pay at the City Hall Tax Office, by mail or by direct debit.

faqs.q: Is the New Rochelle school tax due once a year?
faqs.a: No. It is split into two halves, due on or before September 30 and March 31. The library bill rides along with the school bill.

faqs.q: Who pays the March school installment if I sell in the winter?
faqs.a: That depends on your contract and the closing adjustments. The March bill covers January through June, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will divide it.
